blocks.content: Twelve topics have built a genuine, deep foundation. This final topic answers the most immediately practical question of all: how do you actually start using any of it, hands on, without risking real, unexpected money.
1. AWS Free Tier, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: 1. AWS Free Tier, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: The AWS Free Tier is a set of usage allowances across many popular AWS services, letting a new or existing account use a defined amount of specific services each month without being charged, specifically to support learning and experimentation.

This is not a single, uniform offer. It spans several distinct categories, covered fully in the next section of this topic, each with its own specific rules about how long the free usage lasts and what exactly it covers.

Every hands on example demonstrated conceptually throughout this module, launching an EC2 instance, creating an S3 bucket, can genuinely be tried for real, directly within Free Tier limits, on a new AWS account without incurring any cost.

Understanding Free Tier precisely, including its real limits and real expiration dates, is essential before beginning any hands on practice with the specific services covered across the remaining eighteen modules of this course.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736137383-678306367.png
blocks.alt: AWS Free Tier given its own full depth

blocks.content: 2. Three Categories of Free Tier Offerings
blocks.text: 2. Three Categories of Free Tier Offerings

blocks.content: Always Free offers apply indefinitely, for the lifetime of an AWS account, covering a specific, limited amount of usage for certain services regardless of how long the account has existed, such as a defined monthly allowance of AWS Lambda invocations.

12 Months Free offers apply only during the first twelve months after an account is created, covering a specific amount of usage for certain services, such as a defined number of hours of a small EC2 instance type, specifically to support new account onboarding.

Short Term Trials offer free usage of a specific service for a short, defined period, typically measured in days rather than months, intended to let a new user briefly evaluate a specific, often newer AWS service before committing to it.

Correctly identifying which category a given Free Tier offer falls into is essential for avoiding a genuine, common surprise: assuming an offer is Always Free when it is actually only available during the first twelve months of a specific account's life.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736138907-536305270.png
blocks.alt: Three genuine distinct categories of Free Tier offerings

3. A Real AWS Free Tier Example
blocks.text: 3. A Real AWS Free Tier Example

blocks.content: Consider a new AWS account created specifically to work through the hands on examples in this course, starting with the EC2 launch example demonstrated conceptually earlier in the What is Cloud Computing topic of this module.

Launching a single t2.micro EC2 instance, one of the specific instance types covered under the 12 Months Free category, and running it for a modest number of hours per month stays comfortably within Free Tier limits, incurring genuinely zero cost.

That same account can also create an S3 bucket and store a small amount of data, covered under its own specific Free Tier allowance, again incurring zero cost as long as usage stays within the documented limits for that specific service.

This combination, one Free Tier eligible EC2 instance and one Free Tier eligible S3 bucket, is genuinely sufficient to work through a meaningful portion of the hands on examples referenced conceptually throughout this entire course's early modules.

# Launch a Free Tier eligible instance type
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abcdef1234567890 --instance-type t2.micro --count 1

# Create an S3 bucket within Free Tier storage limits
aws s3 mb s3://my-learning-bucket-12345

blocks.content: 4. Recap: Pricing Models, Now Made Genuinely Risk Free
blocks.text: 4. Recap: Pricing Models, Now Made Genuinely Risk Free

blocks.content: The previous topic covered four AWS pricing models, On Demand, Reserved Instances, Spot Instances, and Savings Plans, each requiring at least some real spending once usage exceeds the specific allowances covered in this topic.

Free Tier is genuinely the safest possible starting point for learning those exact same services and pricing concepts hands on, specifically because it lets real, genuine usage happen without any of those four pricing models ever actually charging anything.

This connection matters practically: the instance types and usage patterns demonstrated throughout this course's hands on examples are frequently chosen deliberately to align with Free Tier eligible options, specifically to support genuinely risk free learning.

Understanding both topics together, pricing models and Free Tier, gives a complete picture: start free and risk free while learning, then apply the pricing model knowledge from the previous topic deliberately once real, production usage begins.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736142088-719481251.png
blocks.alt: Recap of pricing models, already covered above, now made genuinely risk free

blocks.content: 5. Setting Up Billing Alerts Before Any Experimentation
blocks.text: 5. Setting Up Billing Alerts Before Any Experimentation

blocks.content: Before launching a single resource for hands on learning, configuring a billing alarm through AWS Budgets is a genuinely essential first step, providing an automatic notification if actual spending ever exceeds a threshold you define, such as one dollar.

This alarm acts as a safety net specifically against the common mistake covered later in this topic, accidentally exceeding a Free Tier limit or accidentally leaving a non Free Tier eligible resource running, catching the issue quickly rather than after a full month has already elapsed.

Setting this up takes only a few minutes within the AWS Billing console, and it is a small, one time investment that provides ongoing protection across every subsequent hands on example worked through throughout this entire course.

This habit, configuring monitoring before taking a potentially risky action, mirrors a theme already established elsewhere in this module, particularly around monitoring and reviewing architecture proactively rather than reactively after a problem has already occurred.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736143605-712536820.png
blocks.alt: A billing alarm configured before any Free Tier experimentation

blocks.content: 6. A Common Mistake: Forgetting to Delete Resources
blocks.text: 6. A Common Mistake: Forgetting to Delete Resources

blocks.content: A very common mistake, and the single most frequent cause of unexpected charges on an otherwise Free Tier eligible account, is forgetting to delete or stop resources after finishing a specific hands on exercise or after a short term trial period ends.

An EC2 instance left running past its Free Tier eligible hours, or a short term trial resource left active past its trial period, begins accruing real charges silently, often unnoticed until a monthly billing statement arrives with an unexpected amount.

This mistake is entirely preventable with two habits already covered in this topic: setting up billing alerts before experimentation begins, and deliberately reviewing and cleaning up resources immediately after finishing any specific hands on exercise.

Building both habits now, at the very start of this course, before working through the specific hands on examples referenced conceptually throughout the remaining eighteen modules, prevents this exact, entirely avoidable mistake from ever becoming a real, unpleasant surprise.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736145197-304229291.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of forgetting to delete Free Tier resources after the trial period ends

blocks.content: 7. Setting Up a New AWS Account Correctly
blocks.text: 7. Setting Up a New AWS Account Correctly

blocks.content: Creating a new AWS account for hands on learning requires a valid payment method, even though Free Tier usage itself incurs no charge, since AWS uses this payment method to bill for any usage that genuinely exceeds Free Tier limits.

AWS accounts also include a root user, with full, unrestricted access to everything in that account, and a genuinely important early best practice, covered in complete depth in the very next module, is creating a separate, more limited IAM user for day to day work rather than using the root user directly.

This root user versus IAM user distinction is worth flagging even in this Free Tier topic, since it directly affects how the very first hands on exercises in this course should genuinely be approached from the account's initial creation onward.

Setting up multi factor authentication on the root user immediately after account creation, before any hands on experimentation begins, is a small additional step that meaningfully improves account security from the very start.
8. A Second Real Example: Learning Multiple Services Together
blocks.text: 8. A Second Real Example: Learning Multiple Services Together

blocks.content: Consider a learner working through this course's hands on examples across several modules: an EC2 instance from this module, an S3 bucket for storage, and later, a small Lambda function for the Serverless Architecture module.

Each of these resources typically falls under its own specific Free Tier allowance, and understanding that these allowances are independent, not sharing some combined single pool, matters directly for accurately predicting whether a specific combination of hands on exercises will genuinely remain free.

Checking each specific service's own Free Tier documentation, rather than assuming a single, uniform limit applies universally across every AWS service, avoids a subtle but genuinely common source of confusion for learners new to AWS.

This example reinforces a theme already established elsewhere in this module: checking AWS's own current, authoritative documentation directly, rather than relying on a general impression or an assumption carried over from a different specific service.
9. What Happens When a Free Tier Limit Is Exceeded
blocks.text: 9. What Happens When a Free Tier Limit Is Exceeded

blocks.content: Exceeding a specific Free Tier limit does not typically stop a resource from continuing to run or cause an account to be suspended. It simply means ordinary On Demand charges, covered in complete depth in the previous topic, begin applying to the usage beyond that specific limit.

This is precisely why the billing alert habit covered earlier in this topic matters so directly: without it, usage can genuinely exceed a Free Tier limit and continue accruing real charges for an extended period before anyone notices.

Understanding this behavior, gradual, ordinary charging rather than an abrupt service interruption, sets accurate expectations and reinforces why proactive monitoring, rather than reactive discovery after a bill arrives, is the genuinely correct approach.

This connects directly back to the pricing models topic immediately preceding this one: Free Tier is not a separate system with its own separate rules for exceeding limits, but an allowance layered cleanly on top of the exact same On Demand pricing already covered there.
10. Free Tier as a Genuine On Ramp, Not a Permanent Solution
blocks.text: 10. Free Tier as a Genuine On Ramp, Not a Permanent Solution

blocks.content: Free Tier is deliberately designed as a learning and evaluation tool, not as a permanent, sustainable way to run genuine production workloads indefinitely, and treating it as such would misunderstand its actual, intended purpose.

As hands on practice throughout this course progresses toward more advanced, production oriented patterns, particularly from Module 13 onward covering high availability and real world scenarios, actual usage will naturally begin exceeding Free Tier limits for many exercises.

This is expected and appropriate. Free Tier's job is specifically to remove the initial barrier to hands on learning covered throughout this module, not to eliminate the real, ongoing cost considerations that genuine production AWS usage always involves.

Understanding this distinction now, at the very start of this course, sets an accurate, realistic expectation for how learning on AWS naturally progresses from genuinely free, low stakes experimentation toward the real, deliberate cost management practices covered fully in Module 15.
11. Checking Current Free Tier Usage

The AWS Billing console includes a dedicated Free Tier usage dashboard, showing exactly how much of each specific Free Tier allowance has been consumed during the current month, directly against the specific limit for each individual service.

Checking this dashboard periodically, particularly after working through a new hands on exercise for the first time, confirms usage is genuinely staying within Free Tier limits rather than assuming it is without any direct verification.

This dashboard is a genuinely more reliable source of truth than manually tracking usage independently, since it reflects AWS's own actual billing calculation directly, rather than an estimate made from outside AWS's own systems.
Combining this periodic dashboard check with the billing alerts covered earlier in this topic provides two independent, complementary layers of protection against any unexpected charge.
12. Best Practices for Using AWS Free Tier
blocks.text: 12. Best Practices for Using AWS Free Tier

blocks.content: Configure a billing alarm through AWS Budgets before launching any resource for hands on learning, treating this as a mandatory first step rather than an optional precaution, exactly as covered earlier in this topic.

Identify which specific Free Tier category, Always Free, 12 Months Free, or Short Term Trial, applies to any resource before launching it, avoiding the confusion covered earlier in this topic between permanent and time limited offers.

Delete or stop resources immediately after finishing a specific hands on exercise, rather than leaving them running indefinitely, directly preventing the single most common cause of unexpected Free Tier related charges.

Check the Free Tier usage dashboard periodically, particularly after trying a new service for the first time, confirming actual usage against AWS's own authoritative tracking rather than relying on assumption alone.

blocks.content: 13. Closing Module One: Fundamentals Now Fully Established
blocks.text: 13. Closing Module One: Fundamentals Now Fully Established

blocks.content: This topic closes Module One, having covered what cloud computing is, why organizations adopt it, the deployment and service models available, the shared responsibility governing security, AWS's global physical infrastructure, and the frameworks and practical tools for building and paying for it.

Every remaining module in this nineteen module course builds directly on this foundation: specific services, specific architectures, and specific best practices, all assuming the vocabulary and mental models established across these thirteen topics.

The next module, Identity and Access Management, covers the single most consequential piece of your own side of the Shared Responsibility Model established earlier in this module, and it is the natural, required next step before touching almost any other AWS service hands on.

Carry this module's foundation forward deliberately. Every service covered from here forward in this course is best understood through the lens this module has spent thirteen topics building: what it costs, where it runs, and who is responsible for securing it.

blocks.content: 14. The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

AWS Free Tier makes genuinely hands on, risk free learning possible across Always Free, 12 Months Free, and Short Term Trial offerings, provided the specific limits and expiration rules for each category are correctly understood.

Forgetting to delete or stop resources after finishing a hands on exercise is the single most common, entirely avoidable cause of unexpected charges, directly preventable through the billing alerts and cleanup habits covered in this topic.

With this topic, Module One is complete. Module Two, Identity and Access Management, is the required, natural next step, covering the single most consequential piece of your own security responsibility established earlier in this module.
Keep the billing alert habit firmly in mind above everything else covered in this topic. It is the single cheapest, highest value safeguard available before beginning any hands on AWS learning.
Module One, AWS Fundamentals, is now complete in full, dedicated depth across all thirteen of its topics.
Forward into Module Two: Identity and Access Management, the required, non optional next step before touching almost any other AWS service hands on.
Set the billing alarm first. Everything else in this course can wait five minutes for that.
Delete resources immediately after every exercise. It is the single cheapest habit in this entire module.

points: AWS Free Tier spans three categories, Always Free, 12 Months Free, and Short Term Trials, each with its own specific rules about duration and coverage.
Configuring a billing alarm through AWS Budgets before any hands on experimentation is a mandatory first safeguard against unexpected charges.
Forgetting to delete or stop resources after finishing an exercise is the most common, entirely avoidable cause of unexpected Free Tier related charges.
The Free Tier usage dashboard in the AWS Billing console provides an authoritative, periodic check against AWS's own actual usage tracking.
This closes Module One (AWS Fundamentals) in full. Module Two, Identity and Access Management, is the required next step before working hands on with nearly any other AWS service.
